item.content:encoded:
The University of Bonn and Bonn-Rhein-Sieg University of Applied Sciences are inviting applications for 10 doctoral research positions under the DFG Research Training Group (RTG) “Urban Future – Managing Transformations for Better Health in Blue Cities.”

The interdisciplinary doctoral programme focuses on the relationship between urbanisation, water, public health, ecological sustainability and social justice, with particular attention to cities located along rivers and coastlines.

Starting in April 2027, successful candidates will join a structured four-year doctoral programme that combines individual PhD research with interdisciplinary training, seminars, systems-thinking approaches, transdisciplinary research methods and professional development.

The programme is particularly relevant to graduates interested in urban health, public health, climate change, water-health systems, governance, environmental sustainability, infectious diseases, urban planning, ecological systems, development studies and social sciences.

Successful doctoral researchers will receive a four-year doctoral support contract with remuneration based on TV-L pay grade 13 (65%), according to the German public-sector salary scale. Employment will be at either the University of Bonn or Bonn-Rhein-Sieg University of Applied Sciences.

The application deadline is 19 October 2026.

About the Urban Future Research Training Group

The DFG Research Training Group “Urban Future” examines how cities can manage urban transformations in ways that improve public health, ecological sustainability and social equity.

The programme uses the concept of the “Blue City” to describe urban areas situated along rivers or coastlines where water is considered more than simply a resource or a potential hazard. Instead, water becomes an integral part of:

  • Urban planning
  • Infrastructure development
  • Environmental management
  • Public health
  • Social systems
  • Urban identity
  • Climate adaptation
  • Ecological sustainability

The research programme recognises that cities are complex systems in which environmental, social, economic, political and health-related factors interact.

Researchers will therefore investigate the connections between urban transformation, water-related challenges and health outcomes, particularly in rapidly changing urban environments.

A major emphasis is placed on cities in the Global South, which serve as important living laboratories for understanding urban transformation and developing solutions that can contribute to healthier and more sustainable cities.

However, applicants are not restricted to research sites in the Global South. Candidates are free to propose research sites in any Blue City worldwide, provided that the proposed research aligns with the objectives of the programme.

Universities and International Research Network

The Research Training Group is jointly operated by:

  • University of Bonn
  • Bonn-Rhein-Sieg University of Applied Sciences

It works in cooperation with the German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS) and a network of international partner universities.

The international partnership includes institutions in:

  • Ghana
  • Togo
  • Cameroon
  • Brazil
  • Japan

The listed partner institutions include:

  • KNUST – Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana
  • University of Ghana, Ghana
  • University of Cape Coast, Ghana
  • University of Lomé, Togo
  • University of Buea, Cameroon
  • University of São Paulo, Brazil
  • The University of Tokyo, Japan

This international structure gives doctoral researchers an opportunity to work within a research environment that connects European and Global South perspectives on urban health, sustainability and transformation.

Four Research Themes of the Urban Future PhD Programme

The doctoral programme is organised around four major interdisciplinary research themes.

Research Theme A: Urban Health Resilience

The Urban Health Resilience theme examines how urban communities respond to and recover from health pressures associated with water and environmental change.

Research may focus on issues such as:

  • Flooding
  • Drought
  • Urban heat islands
  • Air pollution
  • Unequal access to clean water
  • Food systems
  • Environmental exposures
  • Mental health
  • Social inequalities
  • Climate adaptation
  • Green and blue infrastructure

The research theme combines perspectives from areas such as epidemiology, sociology, environmental science, urban planning and public health.

Researchers will examine how communities can develop greater resilience while ensuring that vulnerable populations are not left behind.

Example PhD research topics

Potential research areas include:

Urban Food Systems

Possible methods include:

  • Nutritional analysis
  • Dietary surveys
  • Health outcome measurements
  • Intervention studies

Soil Health and Soil Functions

Potential methods include:

  • Soil surveys
  • Soil health indicator measurement
  • Ecosystem measurements
  • Functional measurements

One Health and Planetary Health Resilience

Potential methods include:

  • Human and mental health assessments
  • Environmental exposure measurements
  • Longitudinal studies
  • Spatial analysis
  • Socio-ecological analysis
  • Intervention and transformative studies

Urban Blue and Green Infrastructure

Potential methods include:

  • Health impact assessments
  • Human and mental health assessments
  • Environmental exposure measurements
  • Knowledge, Attitudes and Practices (KAP) surveys
  • Perception surveys
  • Spatial analysis
  • Ecosystem services accounting

Potential supervisors

Research Theme A includes supervision from:

  • Prof. Dr. Ina Danquah
  • PD Dr. Timo Falkenberg
  • Prof. Dr. Martin Hamer
  • Prof. Wiltrud Terlau
  • Prof. Dr. Mariele Evers

Research Theme B: Urban Disease Ecology

The Urban Disease Ecology theme explores how environmental and ecological conditions in urban water landscapes affect disease transmission and human health.

The theme is particularly concerned with:

  • Water-borne diseases
  • Vector-borne diseases
  • Infectious diseases
  • Climate-related health risks
  • Water quality
  • Urban morphology
  • Land-use changes
  • Urban density
  • Pathogen transmission
  • Antimicrobial resistance

The research takes a One Health approach, recognising the interconnected relationship between human health, animals and the environment.

Researchers may investigate how changes in urban development, water management and environmental conditions affect the spread of infectious diseases.

Example PhD research topics

Antimicrobial Resistance

Possible methods include:

  • Microbiological sampling
  • Cultural analysis
  • Molecular analysis
  • Resistance profiling
  • Surveys
  • Water quality analysis
  • Transmission modelling
  • Impact modelling

Helminth Infections and Non-Communicable Diseases

Potential methods include:

  • Parasitological analysis
  • Microbiological analysis
  • Immunological analysis
  • Clinical examinations
  • Biomarker analysis
  • Mouse models for mechanistic research

Urban Microbiome and Dietary Ecology

Potential methods include:

  • Microbiome sequencing
  • Dietary pattern analysis
  • Metagenomic analysis
  • Computational analysis

Vector-Borne Disease

Potential methods include:

  • Climate monitoring
  • Entomological surveys
  • Temperature mapping
  • Vector modelling
  • Pathogen detection

Potential supervisors

Research Theme B includes:

  • Prof. Dr. Christian Borgemeister
  • Prof. Dr. Achim Hörauf
  • Prof. Dr. Marc Hübner
  • Dr. Indulekha Karunakaran
  • Prof. Dr. Nico Mutters
  • PD Dr. Marijo Parcina
  • Dr. Manuel Ritter
  • Prof. Dr. Marie-Christine Simon
  • Dr. Nicole Zacharias

Research Theme C: Governance and Institutional Change

The Governance and Institutional Change theme is particularly relevant to applicants interested in policy, governance, economics, development studies, political science, institutional systems and public-sector transformation.

This research theme examines how political, institutional and societal structures influence urban transformation and the ability of cities to respond to health and environmental challenges.

Areas of interest include:

  • Urban governance
  • Water-health governance
  • Public policy
  • Institutional design
  • Policy instruments
  • Inter-sectoral collaboration
  • Financing mechanisms
  • Participatory decision-making
  • Climate adaptation
  • Population growth
  • Unequal resource distribution
  • Political economy
  • Technological change
  • Healthcare policy
  • Institutional transformation

The research seeks to generate evidence that can support more inclusive, transparent and adaptive approaches to urban development.

Example PhD research topics

Biodiversity-Based Bio-Economies

Possible methods include:

  • Economic impact assessment
  • Policy analysis
  • Value-chain analysis

Cross-Sectoral Governance

Potential methods include:

  • Stakeholder mapping
  • Policy analysis
  • Governance framework development
  • Case studies

Urban Transformation and Pharmaceutical Innovation

Potential methods include:

  • Case study analysis
  • Technology assessment
  • Policy evaluation
  • Innovation studies

Political Economy of Health Equity and Technological Change

Potential methods include:

  • Political economy analysis
  • Institutional economics
  • Policy process tracing
  • Case studies
  • Impact analysis

Urban Healthcare Policy Implementation

Potential methods include:

  • Institutional economics
  • Case studies
  • Impact analysis
  • Microeconometric evaluation

Climate-Responsive Health Policy

Potential methods include:

  • Policy mapping
  • Infrastructure mapping
  • Spatial analysis
  • Policy evaluation
  • Implementation research
  • Economic impact assessment

Potential supervisors

Research Theme C includes:

  • Prof. Dr. Katja Bender
  • Prof. Dr. Jan Börner
  • Prof. Dr. Anna-Katharina Hornidge
  • Prof. Dr. Simona Helmsmüller
  • Dr. Christoph Strupat

Research Theme D: Adaptive Urban Ecosystems

The Adaptive Urban Ecosystems theme focuses on how cities can plan and manage ecological and blue-green infrastructure in response to climate change and socio-economic transformation.

Research areas include:

  • Urban land-use systems
  • Water infrastructure
  • Nature-based solutions
  • Ecosystem resilience
  • Climate adaptation
  • Circular economy
  • Integrated water-resource management
  • Biodiversity
  • Urban soil management
  • Ecosystem services
  • Sustainable urban development

This theme brings together engineering, ecological and planning perspectives to investigate how urban environments can be designed to provide multiple benefits for both people and ecosystems.

Example PhD research topics

Coupling Mechanisms of Urbanization

Potential methods include:

  • Hydrological modelling
  • System-dynamics modelling
  • Ecosystem-services analysis

Biodiversity and Human Wellbeing

Potential methods include:

  • Biodiversity surveys
  • Spatial data analysis
  • Socioeconomic surveys

Urban Soil Management

Potential methods include:

  • Soil sampling
  • Soil biodiversity surveys
  • Morphological identification
  • Molecular identification
  • Soil health indicators
  • Spatial analysis

Urban Decision Environments

Potential methods include:

  • Coupled ecological-economic systems modelling
  • Collective learning dynamics

One Planetary Health

Potential methods include:

  • Integrated modelling
  • Framework development
  • Systems thinking
  • Commons governance studies

Potential supervisors

Research Theme D includes:

  • Prof. Dr. Wolfram Barfuss
  • Dr. Bibiana Betancur
  • Prof. Dr. Lisa Biber-Freudenberger
  • Prof. Dr. Mariele Evers

What Does the PhD Programme Offer?

Successful candidates will receive a structured doctoral research experience rather than simply conducting an independent PhD project.

The programme provides several forms of academic and professional support.

1. Four-Year Doctoral Support Contract

The Research Training Group will begin on 1 April 2027.

Successful applicants will receive a four-year doctoral support contract, with remuneration dependent on TV-L pay grade 13 at 65%, in accordance with the German public salary scale.

Employment will be at either:

  • University of Bonn; or
  • Bonn-Rhein-Sieg University of Applied Sciences.

2. Funded Research Expenses

The programme states that fieldwork, travel and related research expenses are fully funded.

This is particularly important for doctoral projects involving international fieldwork or research in different urban environments.

3. Structured Doctoral Training

Doctoral researchers will participate in an interdisciplinary training programme covering areas such as:

  • Systems thinking
  • Transdisciplinary research
  • Academic communication
  • Interdisciplinary research
  • Research methods
  • Soft skills
  • Professional development

4. Interdisciplinary Research Environment

The programme brings together researchers from different academic disciplines.

This allows doctoral candidates to examine urban health challenges from multiple perspectives rather than approaching them from a single discipline.

5. International Research Network

Researchers will have access to a strong national and international network involving universities and research institutions in Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America.

6. Career Development Support

The programme also provides dedicated career development support, structured supervision and clear progression criteria.

Responsibilities of Selected Doctoral Researchers

Successful candidates will be expected to actively participate in the Research Training Group and contribute to its interdisciplinary research environment.

Their responsibilities will include:

  1. Participating actively in the RTG training programme.
  2. Taking part in interdisciplinary seminars.
  3. Conducting independent doctoral research aligned with one of the four research themes.
  4. Developing appropriate research methodologies.
  5. Collecting and analysing research data.
  6. Publishing research findings.
  7. Contributing to the development of Blue City concepts.
  8. Participating in transdisciplinary knowledge exchange.
  9. Developing systems-thinking and interdisciplinary research capabilities.

Who Can Apply?

The programme is seeking applicants who have already completed a Master’s degree or equivalent qualification in a relevant discipline.

The call specifically identifies a broad range of eligible academic backgrounds.

These include:

  • Agricultural and Food Systems
  • Climate and Earth Sciences
  • Development Studies
  • Ecology and Life Sciences
  • Economics and Management
  • Mathematics
  • Physics
  • Computer Science
  • Environmental Sciences
  • Health Sciences
  • Geography
  • Infectious Diseases
  • Hygiene and Infection Control
  • Medical Microbiology
  • Public Health
  • Urban and Regional Studies
  • Social Sciences

Applicants should also demonstrate:

  • A strong interdisciplinary mindset
  • A clear interest in urban transformation
  • Interest in the water-health nexus and/or urban health
  • Excellent written English
  • Excellent spoken English

English Language Requirement

Applicants are required to provide evidence of English language proficiency at B2 level, according to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR), or an equivalent qualification such as TOEFL.

Is the Opportunity Open to International Applicants?

Yes. The programme has an explicitly international research orientation and involves partner institutions across Africa, Asia, Latin America and Europe.

The call identifies partner institutions in Ghana, Togo, Cameroon, Brazil and Japan, while applicants are permitted to propose research sites in any Blue City worldwide.

Therefore, the programme is not presented as being restricted to German or European applicants.

Applicants should, however, ensure that they satisfy the academic, language and application requirements specified in the official call.

Application Documents Required

The application process consists of two stages.

Applications will first be assessed by the RTG Selection Committee. Candidates considered among the most qualified will then be invited to participate in a virtual interview.

Applicants are required to submit the following:

1. Curriculum Vitae

A tabular-format CV should be provided, presenting the applicant’s academic background, professional experience, research experience, skills and other relevant information.

2. Degree Certificates and Transcripts

Applicants must provide:

  • Higher education degree certificate(s)
  • Full transcript(s) of records
  • An explanation of the grading system used for previous studies

3. Motivation Letter

A motivation letter of no more than 500 words is required.

The letter should explain the applicant’s motivation for joining the programme and demonstrate their interest in the relevant research area.

4. Research Exposé

Applicants must submit a research exposé of no more than 1,500 words.

This is an important part of the application because candidates are expected to propose doctoral research aligned with one of the programme’s four research themes.

5. Interdisciplinary Research Statement

Applicants must provide an interdisciplinary research statement of no more than 500 words.

This should demonstrate their ability to think across disciplinary boundaries and connect their proposed research with the wider objectives of the Research Training Group.

6. Letter of Recommendation

Applicants must submit one letter of recommendation.

7. English Language Certificate

Applicants must provide evidence of B2-level English proficiency, such as CEFR, TOEFL or an equivalent qualification.

Application Deadline

The deadline to submit a complete application is:

19 October 2026

Applicants should ensure that all required documents are prepared and submitted through the online application portal before the deadline.

Candidates should also indicate the specific research theme they are applying for.

Important Information About Gender Equality

The call states that, in accordance with the Landesgleichstellungsgesetz (LGG) NRW, women will be given preference in cases where candidates have equal suitability, qualifications and professional performance, unless reasons relating to another candidate prevail.

The programme also states that it is committed to diversity and equal opportunity and is certified as a family-friendly university.

Why the Blue City Concept Matters

The Blue City concept is central to the programme.

Rather than treating water solely as something that cities need to control, remove or supply, the programme examines water as an important component of the urban environment.

This approach can involve examining:

  • Rivers
  • Coastlines
  • Flood management
  • Water infrastructure
  • Public health
  • Urban ecosystems
  • Climate resilience
  • Green-blue infrastructure
  • Water quality
  • Urban planning
  • Social equity
  • Disease ecology
  • Governance

The programme therefore recognises that water-related challenges cannot always be addressed through engineering solutions alone.

They may also require changes in governance, public policy, community participation, health systems, environmental management and urban planning.

Potential Research Opportunities for Social Science Graduates

One notable aspect of this doctoral programme is its interdisciplinary structure.

Applicants from social-science backgrounds can potentially find relevant research opportunities, particularly within Research Cluster C: Governance and Institutional Change.

Relevant areas include:

  • Cross-sectoral governance
  • Political economy
  • Health policy
  • Institutional economics
  • Policy implementation
  • Climate-responsive health policy
  • Urban transformation
  • Technological change
  • Stakeholder participation
  • Institutional design

This means that candidates do not necessarily need a medical or laboratory-science background to be relevant to the programme, provided their academic background and proposed research align with one of the eligible areas.

Research Sites Can Be Located Worldwide

Although the Research Training Group places particular emphasis on cities in the Global South, applicants are free to propose research sites in any Blue City worldwide.

This provides considerable flexibility when developing a doctoral research proposal.

Applicants could therefore potentially develop projects examining urban health and water-related challenges in different geographical contexts, provided the proposed research fits the programme’s objectives and one of its four research themes.

Application Process

Applicants should follow these steps:

Step 1: Select a Research Theme

Review the four research themes:

  1. Urban Health Resilience
  2. Urban Disease Ecology
  3. Governance and Institutional Change
  4. Adaptive Urban Ecosystems

Choose the theme that most closely corresponds to your academic background and proposed doctoral research.

Step 2: Develop Your Research Idea

Prepare a research proposal that addresses a relevant urban-health challenge and demonstrates a clear connection to the selected research theme.

Step 3: Prepare the Required Documents

Prepare:

  • CV
  • Degree certificate(s)
  • Full transcript(s)
  • Grading-system explanation
  • Motivation letter
  • Research exposé
  • Interdisciplinary research statement
  • Recommendation letter
  • English-language certificate

Step 4: Submit the Online Application

Submit the complete application through the official University of Bonn application portal.

Step 5: Selection and Interview

The Selection Committee will evaluate applications.

Shortlisted candidates will be invited to a virtual interview.

Key Facts at a Glance

Information Details
Programme DFG Research Training Group “Urban Future”
Main focus Urban health and transformations in Blue Cities
Institution University of Bonn and Bonn-Rhein-Sieg University of Applied Sciences
Opportunity Doctoral research positions
Number of positions 10
Duration 4 years
Start date 1 April 2027
Remuneration TV-L pay grade 13 (65%)
Research expenses Fieldwork, travel and related research expenses funded
Degree areas Multiple disciplinary faculties/Promotionskolleg NRW
English requirement B2 CEFR, TOEFL or equivalent
Application format Two-stage selection
Interview Virtual interview for selected candidates
Application deadline 19 October 2026
Research locations Any Blue City worldwide
International focus Strong focus on Global South and international partnerships

Conclusion

The Urban Future DFG Research Training Group offers an interdisciplinary doctoral research opportunity for graduates interested in understanding how cities can respond to interconnected challenges involving water, public health, climate change, environmental sustainability and social equity.

With 10 doctoral positions, a four-year support contract, funding for fieldwork and travel, structured doctoral training, interdisciplinary supervision and an international research network, the programme provides a research environment that brings together natural sciences, health sciences, economics, governance, social sciences, environmental research and urban studies.

The four research themes—Urban Health Resilience, Urban Disease Ecology, Governance and Institutional Change, and Adaptive Urban Ecosystems—provide applicants with several pathways for developing a doctoral research project.

Candidates interested in applying should carefully select the research theme that matches their academic background and research interests, prepare the required documents and submit their complete application by 19 October 2026.

item.content:encoded:
The African Development Bank (AfDB) and the UNDP AI Hub for Sustainable Development, in partnership with Google and Apolitical, are offering a free, world-class artificial intelligence training opportunity designed specifically for government officials and public servants.

The initiative aims to strengthen AI capabilities within the public sector, helping government professionals understand artificial intelligence, identify practical applications, manage risks, and support responsible AI adoption in government institutions.

As governments across Africa and around the world increasingly explore artificial intelligence for public service delivery, policymaking, procurement, healthcare, climate action and organisational transformation, the programme provides public servants with practical knowledge they can use in their daily work.

Applications are currently open, with a deadline of 30 September 2026.

About the Government AI Training Initiative

The initiative is being delivered through the Apolitical Government AI Campus, a global learning platform focused on building AI capabilities within government.

The African Development Bank is a founding member of the AI Hub’s Executive Steering Group, while the UNDP AI Hub for Sustainable Development is partnering with Google and Apolitical to deliver public-sector AI capability building.

The broader Government AI Campus seeks to prepare 1 million public servants to lead effectively in the age of artificial intelligence.

The Campus is supported by Google.org and the Rockefeller Foundation and is designed to be technology-agnostic. This means that the training is not focused on promoting a single AI technology or platform. Instead, it helps government leaders and practitioners understand AI, use it responsibly and explore how it can contribute to better public-sector outcomes.

The programme is particularly relevant as governments seek to close AI capability gaps and strengthen cooperation between the public sector, private-sector partners and innovation ecosystems.

Why This AI Training Matters for Public Servants

Artificial intelligence is increasingly being explored across government operations, including public administration, procurement, healthcare, climate policy, service delivery and strategic decision-making.

However, effective AI adoption requires more than access to technology. Public servants also need to understand:

  • What artificial intelligence can and cannot do
  • How AI systems work
  • How to identify appropriate government use cases
  • The ethical and legal implications of AI
  • Privacy and fairness considerations
  • How to evaluate AI-generated information
  • How to use generative AI responsibly
  • How AI can improve public-service delivery
  • How organisations can develop AI-ready workforces
  • How governments can manage the risks associated with AI adoption

The Government AI Campus seeks to address these capability gaps through accessible, practical and self-paced training.

According to the programme information, 84% of Campus users say the training made them more effective at their jobs, while 87% say the training was relevant to their daily work.

What Is Offered?

Selected applicants will receive access to a curated set of courses from the Apolitical Government AI Campus.

The training is designed to accommodate busy government professionals. Rather than requiring participants to attend scheduled lectures or live sessions, the courses can be completed online at the participant’s own pace.

Flexible and Self-Paced Learning

The courses are:

  • Fully online
  • Self-paced
  • Accessible from any device
  • Designed without mandatory live sessions
  • Not tied to a fixed class schedule
  • Suitable for professionals balancing work and learning

Most courses take approximately two to three hours to complete.

Participants can start a course, pause their learning and return later. Their progress is automatically saved, allowing them to fit the training around their professional responsibilities.

Core Courses Available Through the Programme

The initiative features seven core courses covering different aspects of artificial intelligence and its application in government.

Course 1: Understand How AI Impacts You and Your Government

This introductory course is designed to help public servants develop a basic understanding of artificial intelligence without requiring prior technical knowledge.

Participants will explore what AI is, what it can do, what its limitations are and why these issues matter for government.

By completing this course, participants will be able to:

  • Define artificial intelligence and explain its capabilities and limitations.
  • Recognise the major benefits and risks associated with AI in the public sector.
  • Identify ways AI can be harnessed for the public good.
  • Explore how AI can contribute to improved public-service delivery.
  • Discuss how public servants can use AI tools responsibly.

This course can therefore serve as an entry point for public servants who are new to artificial intelligence.

Course 2: AI Fundamentals for Public Servants — Opportunities, Risks and Strategies

The second course provides a deeper examination of artificial intelligence.

Powered by content from Stanford Online, the course explores how AI works, what its capabilities and limitations are, and how governments can approach AI adoption in a human-centred manner.

The course also addresses issues surrounding trust, fairness, privacy, ethics and regulation.

Participants will learn how to:

  • Explain the technology behind artificial intelligence.
  • Analyse trust, fairness, privacy and ethical risks associated with AI.
  • Investigate the potential impacts of AI use cases through a human-centred approach.
  • Distinguish ways AI can enhance government work.
  • Apply lessons from AI experiments across different sectors.
  • Consider regulatory frameworks relevant to AI.
  • Explore strategies for responsible AI adoption within government.

This course is particularly relevant for public servants who are expected to participate in discussions or decisions concerning AI adoption.

Course 3: Effective Prompt Engineering for Public Servants

Generative AI tools can produce significantly different results depending on how instructions are written.

This practical course introduces public servants to prompt engineering, helping them communicate more effectively with generative AI systems.

Participants learn how to formulate prompts, assess AI-generated responses and improve their instructions to achieve more useful results.

The course enables participants to:

  • Understand what prompt engineering means.
  • Explain why effective prompting is relevant to government work.
  • Construct effective prompts for interacting with AI.
  • Critically evaluate AI-generated responses.
  • Refine prompts iteratively to improve AI outputs.
  • Apply generative AI more effectively to everyday professional tasks.

For public servants already experimenting with generative AI, these skills can be particularly relevant to improving productivity and the quality of AI-assisted work.

Course 4: AI Leadership in Government — Building Trust, Skills and an Innovative Culture

This course is specifically tailored toward senior officials and leaders responsible for managing teams and shaping organisational culture.

AI adoption is not solely a technology issue. Government institutions also need employees who understand how to use AI and feel confident and safe experimenting with new technologies.

The course therefore focuses on the human and organisational foundations necessary for responsible AI adoption.

Participants will learn how to:

  • Describe the strategic value of AI for government operations.
  • Understand the importance of an AI-ready workforce.
  • Identify approaches for building a workforce that is informed and confident about AI.
  • Develop a workplace culture that encourages innovation and responsible experimentation.
  • Apply strategies for supporting AI adoption within organisations.
  • Create a personalised plan for developing an AI-ready workforce.

The course can be particularly relevant to managers, directors, team leaders and senior public officials involved in organisational transformation.

Course 5: Smarter Procurement with AI

Artificial intelligence has the potential to transform different stages of the public procurement process.

This course examines where AI can potentially improve efficiency and impact within procurement while also addressing the risks associated with using AI in this area.

Participants are introduced to practical frameworks for considering AI applications within procurement.

The course covers:

  • Fundamentals of AI and its application in procurement.
  • Ways AI can address procurement challenges.
  • Opportunities for optimising procurement processes.
  • Ethical considerations surrounding AI in procurement.
  • Legal risks associated with AI adoption.
  • Real-world case studies and best practices.
  • Initial steps for integrating AI into procurement environments.

This course is particularly relevant to public officials working in procurement, contracting, supply-chain management and related administrative functions.

Course 6: AI and the Future of Healthcare Systems

The sixth course focuses on artificial intelligence within healthcare.

Developed with SDA Bocconi School of Management, the course is designed for healthcare practitioners, regulators and policymakers who need to understand the opportunities and challenges presented by AI in healthcare systems.

Participants will explore:

  • The fundamentals of AI.
  • Key characteristics and applications of AI in healthcare.
  • Opportunities for using AI in healthcare systems.
  • Challenges associated with AI-enabled healthcare.
  • Ethical and regulatory considerations.
  • Methods for assessing AI solutions.
  • Responsible implementation of AI healthcare systems.
  • Healthcare system AI readiness.
  • Realistic timelines for AI integration.

The course can therefore provide useful knowledge for professionals involved in healthcare policy, regulation, administration and technology adoption.

Course 7: AI and Climate — Trade-offs and Transformation

The seventh course examines the relationship between artificial intelligence and climate change.

Powered by content from Stanford Online, the course explores how AI can support climate solutions while also examining the environmental costs associated with AI systems.

Participants will consider how AI can contribute to areas such as resilient urban planning and the energy transition.

Participants will learn how to:

  • Explain why AI and climate change are increasingly interconnected.
  • Understand how AI can contribute to climate and energy initiatives.
  • Identify ways governments can support AI-enabled climate solutions.
  • Recognise concerns surrounding the environmental impact of AI.
  • Explore how public servants can contribute to addressing AI’s environmental footprint.
  • Understand the role governments can play in supporting greener AI development and adoption.

This course is particularly relevant to public officials involved in climate policy, environmental planning, energy, sustainability and related areas.

Who Can Apply?

The initiative is open to current government officials and public servants who are working on issues connected to the implementation and adoption of AI in their countries.

The opportunity is intended for public-sector professionals working across areas including:

  • Public services
  • Government administration
  • AI implementation
  • Digital transformation
  • Public-sector innovation
  • Public-private partnerships
  • Technology policy
  • Procurement
  • Healthcare
  • Climate and energy
  • Organisational leadership
  • Government strategy

Applicants should be current government officials or public servants whose work relates to AI implementation, public services, partnerships or innovation.

The information provided does not state a specific academic degree requirement, age requirement, gender restriction or professional qualification requirement. It also does not specify a particular nationality restriction within the eligible public-service audience.

Eligibility, Qualifications and Geographic Scope

Eligible Category of People

Current government officials and public servants working on the implementation, adoption or responsible use of AI in their countries.

Academic Qualifications

No specific academic qualification is stated in the provided programme information.

Professional Qualification

Applicants should be current government officials or public servants. The initiative is particularly relevant to people involved in:

  • Public-sector AI
  • Government innovation
  • Public services
  • Public-private partnerships
  • Digital transformation
  • Policy and regulation
  • AI-related implementation

Countries and Continent

The initiative is associated with the UNDP AI Hub for Sustainable Development and African AI development, and the wider programme is aligned with sustainable AI-driven growth in Africa.

The information provided does not give a closed list of eligible African countries or state that applicants must hold a particular nationality. Therefore, applicants should consult the official application form for any country-specific eligibility requirements before applying.

Key Benefits of the Programme

The programme provides several potential benefits for eligible public-sector professionals.

1. Free AI Training

The training is designed to provide selected applicants with access to courses from the Government AI Campus without the normal cost associated with professional learning programmes.

2. Practical Government-Focused AI Knowledge

Rather than focusing solely on technical programming, the courses examine how AI can be understood and applied in real government environments.

3. Flexible Online Learning

Participants can complete the courses remotely and at their own pace.

4. No Fixed Live Class Schedule

Participants do not need to attend live sessions according to a fixed timetable.

5. Training Across Multiple AI Applications

The curriculum covers AI fundamentals, prompt engineering, leadership, procurement, healthcare and climate action.

6. Responsible AI Adoption

The programme places emphasis on issues such as privacy, fairness, trust, ethics, regulation and responsible use.

7. Public-Sector Leadership Development

The leadership course provides senior officials with strategies for creating organisations that are better prepared for AI adoption.

8. Improved Workplace Productivity

The programme reports that 84% of Campus users say the training made them more effective at their jobs, while 87% report that the training was relevant to their daily work.

Why Public Servants May Find the Programme Relevant

The growing adoption of AI means that public servants increasingly need to understand both the opportunities and limitations of AI systems.

A government employee does not necessarily need to become a software engineer to benefit from AI knowledge.

For example, an administrative professional may use AI to support document preparation and information organisation. A procurement officer may need to understand how AI could affect procurement processes. A policymaker may need to evaluate AI-related proposals. A manager may need to lead employees through organisational changes associated with AI adoption.

Similarly, healthcare and climate professionals may need to understand how AI can be responsibly integrated into their respective sectors.

The broad curriculum allows participants to focus on areas that are most relevant to their responsibilities.

Programme Learning Format

The Government AI Campus is designed around accessibility and flexibility.

Participants can:

  1. Access the training online.
  2. Complete courses at their own pace.
  3. Use different devices to access the learning materials.
  4. Pause their studies when necessary.
  5. Return later and continue from where they stopped.
  6. Complete most individual courses within approximately two to three hours.

This format makes the programme particularly suitable for working professionals who may not be able to commit to traditional classroom-based training.

Deadline for Applications

The deadline to apply for the African Development Bank and UNDP AI Hub Government AI Training initiative is:

30 September 2026

Applicants are encouraged to submit their applications before the deadline rather than waiting until the final day.

How to Apply

Interested applicants should complete the official application form provided for the initiative.

Before applying, candidates should ensure that they meet the programme’s eligibility requirements and provide accurate information about their current government or public-service role.

Application Link and Official Website

https://airtable.com/appbhi5ptYm0F6Gxx/paggZpgdfbdtZaJR5/form

OFFICIAL WEBSITE:
https://aihubfordevelopment.org/

For more training programs visit the OFY Website HERE

DEADLINE:
30 September 2026

About the AI Hub for Sustainable Development

The AI Hub for Sustainable Development is involved in initiatives designed to accelerate sustainable AI-driven development, particularly across Africa.

The programme information describes the initiative as a G7-endorsed, MIMIT-UNDP co-led effort aligned with the Italy-Africa Mattei Plan.

The AI Hub’s broader programmes include initiatives focused on areas such as:

  • AI infrastructure
  • Compute readiness
  • Voice AI
  • Cybersecurity
  • Sustainable AI development

These programmes form part of broader efforts to strengthen AI infrastructure, skills and innovation ecosystems.

Other AI Hub Programmes

The AI Hub for Sustainable Development also lists several related programmes, including:

AI Infrastructure Builder

An initiative focused on developing AI infrastructure capabilities.

Compute Accelerator Programme — Compute Ready

A programme addressing compute-related readiness and AI infrastructure requirements.

Voice AI Pathways

An initiative focused on expanding voice AI applications to underserved communities.

Cyber4Africa

A programme focused on cybersecurity and related digital capabilities across Africa.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this a scholarship?

No. The opportunity is a free professional training programme, rather than a traditional academic scholarship.

Is the training online?

Yes. The courses are fully online and self-paced.

Do participants need to attend live classes?

No. The programme information states that participants do not need to attend live sessions or follow a fixed schedule.

How long do the courses take?

Most individual courses take approximately two to three hours to complete.

Do applicants need previous AI experience?

Not necessarily. The first course is specifically designed to explain AI in plain language and does not require prior technical knowledge.

Can senior government officials participate?

Yes. One of the courses is specifically designed for senior officials who manage teams and influence organisational culture.

Is there a course specifically about procurement?

Yes. Course 5, Smarter Procurement with AI, focuses on AI applications, risks and opportunities within procurement.

Is healthcare covered?

Yes. Course 6, AI and the Future of Healthcare Systems, focuses on AI applications and responsible implementation in healthcare.

Is climate change covered?

Yes. Course 7, AI and Climate: Trade-offs and Transformation, examines both the potential benefits of AI for climate action and its environmental costs.

What is the application deadline?

The application deadline is 30 September 2026.

Conclusion

The African Development Bank, UNDP AI Hub for Sustainable Development, Google and Apolitical’s Government AI training initiative provides public servants with an opportunity to develop practical knowledge about artificial intelligence and its application in government.

Through the Apolitical Government AI Campus, selected participants can access a range of self-paced courses covering AI fundamentals, prompt engineering, government leadership, procurement, healthcare and climate action.

The programme goes beyond simply explaining AI technology. It also addresses responsible AI adoption, including issues such as privacy, fairness, trust, ethics, regulation and organisational readiness.

For current government officials and public servants whose work intersects with AI implementation, public services, innovation or public-private partnerships, the training provides a structured way to build relevant AI knowledge while continuing with their professional responsibilities.

The application deadline is 30 September 2026.

Applicants should review the official application requirements and submit their applications through the designated application form before the deadline.

item.content:encoded:
The LabStart Fellowship 2027 is inviting entrepreneurs and aspiring founders with a passion for climate technology and entrepreneurship to apply for its next cohort. The program is designed to help entrepreneurs turn promising climate technologies and research into viable startups by providing funding, training, mentorship, access to technologies, and connections across the climate innovation ecosystem.

Applications for the 2027 cohort are currently open, with a deadline of October 9, 2026.

LabStart focuses on bridging the gap between promising technologies developed in research laboratories and their commercialization in the market. Its program connects entrepreneurs with technologies, researchers, technology-transfer offices, industry experts, investors, and other stakeholders who can help transform an early-stage idea into a functioning climate technology company.

What Is the LabStart Fellowship?

The LabStart Fellowship is a climate technology entrepreneurship program designed to help founders move from an early-stage concept or technology opportunity toward launching a company.

The program focuses particularly on deep climate technology, including technologies emerging from research laboratories and universities.

Rather than requiring every applicant to arrive with a fully developed company, LabStart describes several situations in which its program can be useful. These include entrepreneurs who:

  • Want to start a climate technology company but have not yet identified the ideal technology or business opportunity.
  • Have identified a promising technology but need help obtaining a license.
  • Have not yet raised capital for a specific product or technology.
  • Are exploring a new market or innovative climate solution.
  • Want to spin a technology out of a laboratory or university.
  • Are looking for technologies to commercialize but have not yet identified the right market.

The fellowship therefore focuses on helping entrepreneurs navigate the difficult journey between technology development, commercialization, company formation, and market entry.

LabStart’s Approach to Climate Technology

LabStart’s model is based on the idea that significant climate innovations can remain underdeveloped or under-commercialized when researchers do not have the entrepreneurial expertise, networks, capital, or commercialization pathways required to bring those technologies to market.

The organization works with research laboratories, universities, technology-transfer offices, industry partners, and entrepreneurs to help close this gap.

Its approach includes:

  • Identifying promising climate technologies.
  • Connecting those technologies with entrepreneurs.
  • Helping founders evaluate market opportunities.
  • Supporting intellectual-property and licensing processes.
  • Providing entrepreneurship training.
  • Connecting founders with mentors.
  • Providing funding.
  • Preparing companies for future investment and accelerator opportunities.

What Does the LabStart Fellowship Provide?

The current LabStart program provides a combination of funding, training, mentorship, technology access, and networks.

The official program page describes the fellowship as a 12-month program with access to capital, capacity building, networks, and technology commercialization support.

1. Access to Capital

LabStart provides milestone-based funding to support founders during the early stages of building their companies.

The current program materials describe:

  • $100,000 milestone-based funding on the program page.
  • Full-time funding intended to give founders financial stability while focusing on their startups.

Recent LabStart communications about the 2027–28 cohort have also referred to up to $125,000 in direct and in-kind funding, including support associated with the Discovery and Launch phases.

Because the figures differ across current LabStart materials, applicants should check the latest program and application materials for the exact funding structure applicable to Cohort 2027.

2. Climate Tech Entrepreneurship Training

Fellows receive training focused on climate technology entrepreneurship.

The curriculum is designed to help participants understand how to:

  • Evaluate emerging technologies.
  • Identify market opportunities.
  • Build a commercially viable business.
  • Develop a climate technology startup.
  • Navigate intellectual property.
  • Commercialize research.
  • Grow a company sustainably.

The program’s curriculum is developed and delivered by FRACTAL, whose leaders have experience working with climate technology companies.

3. Expert Mentorship

Participants receive mentorship from experienced climate entrepreneurs and deep-tech professionals.

The mentorship component can help founders understand the practical challenges associated with:

  • Startup development
  • Technology commercialization
  • Market validation
  • Fundraising
  • Intellectual property
  • Business strategy
  • Company growth

LabStart describes its mentor and partner network as an important part of helping entrepreneurs navigate the path from laboratory innovation to market.

4. Access to Research Technologies

One of the defining features of LabStart is its connection to research institutions.

Fellows can receive access to technologies developed through U.S. research institutions and laboratories and can work with researchers and technology-transfer offices to explore commercialization opportunities.

This can be particularly relevant to founders who want to build a company around a technology that has already undergone significant scientific development but still needs an entrepreneur and commercialization strategy.

5. Intellectual Property and Licensing Support

Commercializing laboratory research often requires navigating intellectual-property rights and licensing agreements.

LabStart provides guidance on areas such as:

  • Initial technology licenses
  • Copyright agreements
  • Technology development plans
  • Technology-transfer processes
  • Licensing negotiations
  • Commercialization pathways

The program states that it can also provide financial assistance for initial licensing agreements and consultations.

6. Industry and Investor Networks

LabStart fellows gain access to a network involving:

  • Climate innovators
  • Industry leaders
  • Investors
  • Potential partners
  • Research institutions
  • Technology-transfer offices
  • Incubators
  • Accelerators

These connections can be valuable when founders begin looking for customers, investment, partnerships, technical expertise, or additional startup support.

Who Is LabStart Looking For?

The 2027 application page identifies several characteristics associated with the type of entrepreneur LabStart is seeking.

Passion for Climate and Entrepreneurship

Applicants should demonstrate genuine interest in both:

  • Climate solutions; and
  • Entrepreneurship.

The program is intended for people who want to create businesses capable of addressing climate-related challenges.

Willingness to Launch a Company Full Time

Applicants should be willing and ready to dedicate themselves to launching a company full time.

This is an important commitment because LabStart’s program is designed around founders actively building their ventures rather than participating casually alongside another primary commitment.

Nontraditional and First-Time Founders

LabStart explicitly welcomes people who may not follow the traditional startup-founder profile.

The application page identifies:

  • Nontraditional founders
  • Women
  • BIPOC founders
  • First-time founders

as groups represented in the type of entrepreneurial community LabStart seeks to support.

Previous startup experience is not necessarily required. LabStart’s earlier fellowship announcement specifically stated that previous startup experience was not required and that the program was open to people who wanted to launch climate startups even if they had not yet identified the perfect idea.

APPLY HERE

The LabStart Application Journey

The 2027 application process asks applicants to demonstrate several important elements of their background, experience, entrepreneurial thinking, and climate technology vision.

Step 1: Background

Applicants are asked to showcase their journey and explain the experiences that have contributed to their interest in climate innovation.

This is an opportunity to demonstrate how personal, academic, professional, research, technical, or entrepreneurial experiences have shaped the applicant’s interest in climate technology.

Applicants should be able to explain:

  • What experiences have influenced them.
  • Why climate innovation matters to them.
  • How their previous journey connects to entrepreneurship.
  • What motivates them to build a climate-focused company.

Step 2: Past Experience

Applicants should demonstrate their existing expertise.

This can involve explaining:

  • Previous projects
  • Technical skills
  • Professional experience
  • Research experience
  • Industry knowledge
  • Entrepreneurial experience
  • Relevant scientific or engineering capabilities

The purpose is to demonstrate what the applicant can bring to the development and commercialization of a climate technology.

Step 3: Startup Idea

Applicants must explain their startup vision.

This involves describing a proposed solution to a climate-related problem and explaining how the idea could contribute to addressing climate change.

Applicants should be prepared to communicate:

  • The problem they want to solve.
  • The technology or innovation behind their proposed solution.
  • Who could use the solution.
  • Why the problem matters.
  • How the solution could create value.
  • What makes the approach potentially different or useful.

Step 4: Choose Your Challenge

The program also provides applicants with an opportunity to explore a curated selection of high-potential, licensable technologies.

These technologies are identified and reviewed by LabStart’s laboratory partners and stakeholders.

Applicants can consider these technologies when developing their commercialization strategy or can propose other institutions, technologies, needs, or market gaps they believe should be addressed.

This means applicants do not necessarily have to approach the program with a single fully developed technology already in hand.

Characteristics LabStart Values

LabStart identifies several traits that it looks for in prospective fellows.

Scientific Literacy

Applicants should have the ability to evaluate the potential impact and market opportunity associated with a technology.

Scientific literacy does not simply mean understanding scientific concepts. It also involves being able to connect technology with real-world problems and commercial opportunities.

Entrepreneurial Spirit

Entrepreneurs need the ability to communicate a vision, tell a compelling story, experiment, and make decisions while managing uncertainty and risk.

LabStart identifies entrepreneurial spirit as an important characteristic for fellows.

Grit and Tenacity

Building a climate technology company can involve significant challenges.

LabStart therefore looks for people who are willing to persist when they encounter:

  • Technical obstacles
  • Market challenges
  • Funding difficulties
  • Licensing barriers
  • Business setbacks
  • Other roadblocks

Technological Motivation

Applicants should have a genuine interest in particular technologies or technology fields that could inspire the creation of a new business.

This can be connected to a specific scientific discipline, engineering area, energy technology, materials technology, climate solution, or another relevant field.

Authenticity and Coachability

LabStart values founders who understand their current position and remain open to constructive feedback.

Being coachable can be important because early-stage entrepreneurs frequently need to adapt their assumptions based on information from:

  • Mentors
  • Customers
  • Researchers
  • Investors
  • Industry professionals
  • Team members

Collaborative Mindset

Climate technology commercialization often involves scientists, engineers, entrepreneurs, investors, researchers, customers, and other stakeholders.

LabStart therefore seeks people who can work effectively with diverse teams and make use of collective expertise.

LabStart’s Two-Phase Approach

Recent LabStart communications describe the fellowship as having a Discovery Phase and a Launch Phase.

Discovery Phase

The Discovery Phase is designed to help entrepreneurs explore technologies and determine whether there is a viable technology-market opportunity.

The earlier fellowship structure described this phase as a four-month, part-time program, with funding and training designed to help participants identify emerging laboratory technologies and evaluate their market potential.

Launch Phase

The Launch Phase is focused on moving from exploration toward company creation.

The earlier structure described the Launch Phase as a year-long, full-time program, with significant funding, training, and expert support to develop the solution and build the company.

The current program page similarly describes a 12-month training and support structure and emphasizes the expectation that fellows work full time on launching their companies.

Applicants should check the current Cohort 2027 application materials for the precise phase dates and funding terms.

What Happens During the Program?

LabStart’s curriculum is focused on helping entrepreneurs develop the capabilities needed to take climate technologies from research environments into the market.

Core areas include:

  1. Evaluating emerging laboratory technologies.
  2. Understanding market potential.
  3. Identifying customer needs.
  4. Developing a business model.
  5. Understanding intellectual property.
  6. Navigating licensing.
  7. Developing a commercialization strategy.
  8. Building a climate technology company.
  9. Preparing for future investment.
  10. Developing relationships with investors, industry partners, laboratories, and other stakeholders.

The goal is not simply to create an idea but to help founders develop a pathway toward a viable climate venture.

LabStart’s Climate Technology Focus

LabStart focuses on technologies capable of addressing significant climate and sustainability challenges.

Its fellows and alumni have worked across areas including:

  • Energy
  • Renewable energy
  • Energy storage
  • Advanced materials
  • Industrial decarbonization
  • Carbon reduction
  • Circular materials
  • Recycling
  • Grid modernization
  • Agriculture
  • Sustainable manufacturing
  • Infrastructure
  • Climate adaptation

The program’s current fellows include entrepreneurs working on technologies related to areas such as methane reduction, solar energy, demand-response software, critical minerals, sustainable materials, biofuels, and grid modernization.

Examples of Climate Innovation Supported by LabStart

LabStart’s fellowship community illustrates the range of climate technology ideas that can emerge from the program.

Examples include:

  • Carbon-negative methanol from methane emissions.
  • Technologies designed to improve residential solar adoption.
  • Demand-response software for vertical farming.
  • Algae-based biofuels.
  • Technologies addressing industrial plastics recycling.
  • Low-carbon construction materials.
  • Grid modernization solutions.
  • Technologies addressing data-center sustainability.
  • Solutions focused on industrial decarbonization.

These examples demonstrate that climate technology is a broad field extending well beyond traditional renewable-energy businesses.

Connection to U.S. Research Institutions

A major component of LabStart’s model is its connection to U.S. research laboratories and universities.

The organization has worked with institutions including:

  • National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL)
  • Sandia National Laboratories
  • Oak Ridge National Laboratory
  • Pacific Northwest National Laboratory

These partnerships help create pathways through which entrepreneurs can explore the commercialization of research and technology developed within the U.S. research ecosystem.

Is Previous Startup Experience Required?

No previous startup experience is required according to LabStart’s previous fellowship announcement.

The organization has explicitly highlighted opportunities for first-time founders and people who may not have followed traditional entrepreneurial paths.

This means someone who has strong scientific, technical, research, professional, or industry experience but has never founded a company can still be considered within the program’s target founder community.

Is It Necessary to Already Have a Startup?

Not necessarily.

LabStart specifically describes situations where its program can support people who are still searching for the right technology or market opportunity.

The program may therefore be relevant to someone who:

  • Has a strong climate technology interest but no final startup idea.
  • Has identified a technology but needs help commercializing it.
  • Wants to build a company around laboratory research.
  • Is looking for a technology to commercialize.
  • Is exploring a new market.
  • Has an early-stage company and is looking for a strategic technology or commercialization pathway.

Full-Time Commitment

A major expectation is the ability to work full time on launching the company.

LabStart states that fellows commit to working full time on their company for the year and participating in approximately 6–8 hours per week of LabStart programming and events.

Potential applicants should therefore consider whether they can make the required time commitment before applying.

Information Sessions for Cohort 2027

LabStart has scheduled information sessions for applicants interested in learning more about the 2027 cohort.

The application page lists:

  • September 9 at 9:30 a.m. PT
  • October 6 at 3:00 p.m. PT

These sessions provide an opportunity for prospective applicants to learn more about the program and application process.

Application Deadline

Applications for the LabStart Cohort 2027 must be submitted by:

October 9, 2026

The official LabStart application page currently lists October 9 as the application deadline.

Applicants should submit their materials before the deadline rather than waiting until the final hours.

How to Apply

Applicants can review the program details and submit an application through LabStart’s official application process.

Program information:
LabStart Program Details

Application:
LabStart Application Page

The program’s application page provides the current Cohort 2027 information and links applicants to the application process.

Key Details at a Glance

Category Details
Program LabStart Fellowship
Cohort 2027
Focus Climate technology entrepreneurship
Duration Approximately 12 months of program support
Main objective Launch and commercialize climate technology startups
Funding Current materials describe milestone-based funding; recent 2027 communications reference up to $125,000 in direct and in-kind funding
Training Climate tech entrepreneurship and intellectual property fundamentals
Mentorship Climate founders and deep-tech experts
Technology access U.S. research institutions and laboratories
Licensing support Yes
Investor/industry networks Yes
Full-time commitment Required
Target founders Climate-focused entrepreneurs, including nontraditional and first-time founders
Women/BIPOC Specifically encouraged/represented in the program’s target community
Application deadline October 9, 2026
Program information LabStart website
Application LabStart application page

Who Can Apply?

The program is aimed at entrepreneurs and aspiring founders interested in launching climate technology companies.

The current application materials indicate that suitable applicants should demonstrate:

  • Passion for climate and entrepreneurship.
  • Willingness to launch a company full time.
  • Interest in commercializing climate technology.
  • Relevant experience, expertise, or technical knowledge.
  • Scientific literacy.
  • Entrepreneurial spirit.
  • Persistence and resilience.
  • Motivation to work with technology.
  • Openness to feedback and coaching.
  • Ability to collaborate with diverse teams.

The program specifically welcomes nontraditional founders, women, BIPOC founders, and first-time founders.

Visit HERE to learn more about the LabStart Fellowship 2027

Geographic Eligibility

LabStart’s current program is centered on commercializing technologies from U.S. research laboratories and universities, and external descriptions of the 2027 fellowship identify the program region as the United States.

The materials provided do not state a simple citizenship requirement such as “U.S. citizens only.” Therefore, nationality should not be described as an automatic eligibility requirement based solely on the available information.

However, the program’s focus on U.S. research institutions and the U.S. climate technology ecosystem means applicants should carefully review the current application form for any residency, location, work authorization, company formation, or other geographic requirements that may apply to Cohort 2027.

For applicants outside the United States, including applicants from Africa or Zambia, the available public program information does not establish that they are automatically eligible. The application materials should be checked for the current cohort’s specific geographic requirements before applying.

Race and Demographic Eligibility

LabStart’s application materials specifically mention:

  • Women
  • BIPOC founders
  • Nontraditional founders
  • First-time founders

as part of the founder community it seeks to support.

This does not mean that the program is presented as being exclusively limited to those categories. Rather, LabStart states that it seeks to build diverse cohorts and specifically highlights these groups among the entrepreneurs it wants to support.

The program’s broader selection characteristics remain centered on climate passion, entrepreneurship, technological motivation, scientific literacy, resilience, coachability, and collaboration.

Conclusion

The LabStart Fellowship Cohort 2027 is designed for entrepreneurs who want to turn climate technology opportunities into real companies. The program combines funding, entrepreneurship training, expert mentorship, technology access, intellectual-property guidance, licensing support, and connections to investors and industry partners.

A particularly distinctive aspect of the program is its focus on connecting entrepreneurs with research-based technologies from U.S. laboratories and universities. Rather than focusing solely on conventional startup ideas, LabStart works to identify promising technologies and help entrepreneurs develop commercialization pathways for them.

The program is also designed to accommodate different founder journeys. Applicants do not necessarily need to be experienced startup founders, and LabStart explicitly highlights first-time and nontraditional founders, as well as women and BIPOC entrepreneurs, within the community it seeks to build.

Successful participants are expected to make a significant commitment to the program, including working full time toward launching their company and participating in LabStart programming. The program is therefore intended for people who are ready to move beyond simply exploring entrepreneurship and toward actively building a climate technology venture.

For Cohort 2027, applications close on October 9, 2026. Prospective applicants should review the latest LabStart program and application materials carefully, particularly regarding the current funding structure and any geographic or participation requirements, before submitting their application.
